title: Garuda comes for Rama
hookLine: a great wind over the battlefield, the snakes let go, and Vishnu's own eagle comes for Rama
carry: rama is vishnu, and garuda knows

lines: A GREAT WIND OFF THE SEA.
cards: Night on the battlefield, and the camp is out of ideas. Rama lies bound beside his brother. Sugriva wants to carry them home.

Sushena, the monkey physician, says there are healing herbs on mountains far off in the ocean of milk, and someone should be sent. While they're still talking, the wind changes. A great wind comes off the sea.
Clouds tear open, the waves heave, the hills shake, and trees on the shore bend flat. Something enormous is coming down out of the sky.

teach.b: It's Garuda: the great eagle, king of the birds, blazing like fire.
The moment the serpents feel him coming, they let go. The arrows that were snakes slither off the brothers and flee; in the old stories, serpents and Garuda are enemies.
Garuda bows to the brothers and strokes their faces with his hands, and Valmiki says their wounds close at once, and they rise brighter and stronger than before. Rama, amazed, asks: who are you?
The answer is warm, and mysterious.

teach.h: I'M YOUR FRIEND. DON'T ASK WHY.
teach.b: I'm your friend, Garutman, he says, like your own breath moving outside your body. Then, just when you'd expect him to say why he's come, he doesn't. Don't ask, he says, more or less.

You'll understand when the battle is over. He walks around Rama in a circle of respect, and flies off. The monkey army sees the brothers standing and roars so loud that Ravana hears it inside his palace.
So why would Garuda come, and why the secret?
In Hindu tradition, Garuda is the eagle Vishnu rides. And his promise comes true: when the war is over, Valmiki has Brahma himself tell Rama who he is: Narayana, Vishnu.

teach.h: A REAL MAN, AND VISHNU ON EARTH.
teach.b: Hindus hear the whole Ramayana with both sides at once: a real man in a real war, who never claims to be God, and Vishnu on earth, whose own eagle comes down when he falls.
If a friend ever asks a Hindu kid whether Rama is a hero or a god, this is the answer: both. And this is the scene that shows it.

how: In recitations of the Yuddha Kanda, the Garuda episode comes straight after the brothers' fall, and tellers often slow down at Garuda's refusal to say why he came.

o: a sky chariot the gods send to carry Rama home
the great eagle, king of birds, who frees Rama from the snakes
a storm god whose wind drives Indrajit back to Lanka

p: heard by Ravana in his palace

s: Garuda fights the serpents in a long battle
they flee the moment they feel him coming.
Garuda heals the brothers by touching their faces
their wounds close and they rise stronger than before.
Garuda explains exactly why he came
he tells Rama not to ask, and that he'll understand after the war.

games.q: Garuda tells Rama: don't ask why i came; you'll understand when the battle is over. what does Rama hear after the war?
o: that he is Narayana, Vishnu himself, as Brahma tells him.
that Garuda owed an old debt to King Dasharatha.
that Indrajit's serpents were never real.
games.why: Vishnu's own eagle came for him, and after the war Brahma tells Rama who he is. a real man, and Vishnu on earth.

practice: One of the oldest Vaishnava prayers is just a few words: om namo narayanaya, I bow to Narayana, to Vishnu.

Breathe slowly, and say it softly on each out-breath, picturing the great wind coming in off the sea and the serpents letting go. If you don't pray, picture the wind, and let your breath be the one thing you're not holding on to.

wordCard.voice: Garuda, the great eagle, king of birds and the one Vishnu rides, whose wind makes Indrajit's serpent-arrows let go, and whose touch heals the brothers.

orig.note: Sanskrit Garuḍa: the divine eagle, king of birds; Valmiki also calls him Garutmān and Suparṇa, 'fine-winged'.

carryVoice: Your line: Rama is Vishnu, and Garuda knows. The old story behind the eagle and the snakes comes next. See you then.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 50 (Sushena's advice; Garuda's arrival; the serpents flee; the brothers healed)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 117 (after the war, Brahma tells Rama he is Narayana)
